cards.definition: A microorganism or infectious agent that can cause disease.
Single-celled microorganisms; some species can cause disease.
An infectious agent that must use a host cell to reproduce.
The maintenance of stable internal conditions in the body.
A chemical messenger produced by a gland and transported in the blood.
A simple sugar used as a major energy source by cells.
The main control centre of the nervous system.
Contamination of the environment by harmful substances or materials.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can potentially spread between organisms.
A disease not caused by a pathogen and which cannot spread between people.
Organisms with cell walls containing chitin; some species can cause infections.
Usually single-celled organisms, some of which are parasites that cause disease.
An organism that lives on or inside a host and obtains resources from it.
The process by which a pathogen spreads between hosts.
An organism, such as a mosquito, that carries a pathogen between hosts.
The entry and multiplication of pathogens within a host.
A form of reproduction in which one bacterial cell divides into two cells.
A small ring of bacterial DNA that can carry additional genes.
A change in genetic material that can create variation.
Immediate general defence mechanisms that act against many different pathogens.
An immune response targeted toward a particular pathogen or antigen.
An immune cell that surrounds, engulfs and digests pathogens.
A protein produced by B cells that binds to a specific target on a pathogen.
A type of white blood cell involved in specific immunity.
A lymphocyte that can produce antibodies against specific pathogens.
A lymphocyte that can destroy infected cells or help coordinate immune responses.
A long-lasting immune cell that allows a faster response to a previously encountered pathogen.
The community of microorganisms normally living in and on the body.
Protection that occurs when beneficial microbes occupy space and use resources that pathogens need.
A change in the internal or external environment that produces a response.
A structure or cell that detects a change or stimulus.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response.
The part of a regulatory system that processes information and coordinates a response.
A control mechanism in which a change causes responses that reverse that change.
A mechanism in which a response increases or amplifies the original change.
Maintenance of body temperature within a suitable range.
A receptor that detects changes in temperature.
A region of the brain involved in regulating conditions such as body temperature.
Widening of blood vessels near the skin, increasing heat loss.
Narrowing of blood vessels near the skin, reducing heat loss.
A system of glands that produces hormones to regulate body processes.
An organ that releases hormones directly into the bloodstream.
An endocrine gland that releases hormones controlling several other body functions and glands.
An organ that produces digestive enzymes and hormones including insulin and glucagon.
A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose concentration.
A pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose concentration.
The stored form of glucose found mainly in the liver and muscles.
Clusters of hormone-producing cells within the pancreas.
Pancreatic cells within the islets of Langerhans that produce insulin.
Pancreatic cells within the islets of Langerhans that produce glucagon.
A condition in which blood glucose concentration is too high.
The brain and spinal cord.
The nerves connecting the CNS with the rest of the body.
A specialised cell that carries electrical signals through the nervous system.
A neuron that carries information from receptors toward the CNS.
A neuron that carries signals from the CNS to effectors.
The variety of living organisms within an ecosystem or area.
A measure of how cloudy or unclear water is.
A measure of dissolved inorganic and organic substances within water.
The strip of land alongside a river, stream or other waterway.
A molecule, often on the surface of a pathogen, that can trigger a specific immune response.
The body's ability to resist a particular infection, often because of immune memory.
A large phagocytic immune cell that engulfs pathogens, damaged cells and cellular debris.
A common white blood cell that acts rapidly against invading bacteria and fungi.
A white blood cell involved particularly in responses to parasites and allergic reactions.
A white blood cell that releases substances such as histamine during inflammatory and allergic responses.
A chemical involved in inflammation and allergic responses.
The collection of chemical reactions occurring within cells to maintain life.
Regulation of water and dissolved ion concentrations within the body.
The target level around which a homeostatically controlled condition is maintained.
A condition in which the body's core temperature becomes abnormally high.
A condition in which the body's core temperature becomes dangerously low.
A thyroid hormone that influences metabolic activity and heat production.
A hormone involved in preparing the body to respond rapidly to stressful situations.
A hormone produced by the adrenal glands involved in metabolism, stress and inflammation.
Reduced responsiveness of body cells to insulin, making blood glucose more difficult to regulate.
An autoimmune condition in which pancreatic beta cells are destroyed, greatly reducing insulin production.
A condition involving insulin resistance and sometimes insufficient insulin production.
Pollution entering an environment from a single identifiable source.
Pollution entering an environment from many widespread sources rather than one identifiable location.
Excessive nutrient enrichment of water that promotes increased growth of organisms such as algae and disrupts the ecosystem.
Oxygen present in water and available for aquatic organisms to use in respiration.
The ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic that would normally kill them or stop their growth.
Changes to a pathogen's surface antigens that can make existing immune responses less effective.
A condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own cells or tissues.
The principle that a receptor responds only to molecules or signals with a compatible structure.
The conversion of glucose into glycogen for storage.
The breakdown of glycogen to release glucose when blood glucose is low.
A change in a protein's three-dimensional structure that can cause it to lose its normal function.
A condition in which tissues or an environment have insufficient available oxygen.
A rapid increase in algae, often caused by excess nutrients entering an aquatic ecosystem.
The biological breakdown of dead organic material, often by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
